candidates.gold_standard: Objective orthostatic blood pressure measurements demonstrating a sustained drop in systolic BP ≥20 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥10 mmHg (or symptomatic fall) within 3 minutes of standing — ideally including an immediate post‑void BP measurement that reproduces the hypotensive response.
candidates.prune_reason: Immediate post‑void and orthostatic BP/HR measurements are normal (no ≥20/10 mmHg drop and no symptomatic hypotension), making orthostatic/post‑void hypotension unlikely.

differential_evidence.description: Immediate post‑void and standard orthostatic vital signs (BP/HR lying, immediately after standing and immediately after voiding) — a marked post‑void or orthostatic BP drop supports orthostatic/post‑void hypotension or situational vasodepressor response and argues against a primary arrhythmic cause if reproducible.

Continuous cardiac rhythm monitoring/telemetry, 12‑lead ECG, and event capture (Holter or implantable loop recorder if needed) — documentation of a clinically significant arrhythmia during syncope confirms a cardiac cause; absence of arrhythmia during monitoring makes arrhythmic cause less likely.

Head‑up tilt‑table testing with monitoring of heart rate and BP — reproduction of syncope with classic vasovagal pattern (bradycardia and/or hypotension) supports neurally mediated (micturition) syncope and helps distinguish from arrhythmic syncope.

Resting 12‑lead ECG and transthoracic echocardiogram (and medication review) — ECG/echo evidence of significant conduction disease, ischemia, or structural heart disease (or use of alpha‑blockers, nitrates, diuretics) increases pretest probability of cardiogenic or medication‑induced hypotensive syncope and would shift management toward cardiac evaluation.
